utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Anna Richterova, Julian Nicholls, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Mr. Ackerman back from the States?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the latest information, he'll be back on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I thought he was coming back on Wednesday. All right. Yes, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but can we go to private session at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It concerns the witness next week, 7.144, the UN. Now the open session possibility was granted, he can testify openly. It is the first thing and then I receive information from Ms. Korner that she won't be able to finish her examination-in-chief by Wednesday. It means that there will be probably one more day for cross-examination and maybe even more, and we have another witness who is coming on Friday, and if he is not able to finish his testimony on Friday, then we will have to bring him over two weeks later because we are not sitting in the week starting 17 of February. So Ms. Korner would like to know whether we are still bringing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I mean, is it -- is witness 7.144, is this witness going to take so much of our time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Ms. Korner believes yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't interfere obviously. I mean if Ms. Korner needs three days --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's not three days, it's two days because we are not sitting on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. You are right, you are right. I don't know what to tell you. I mean it's a decision that you have to make. It obviously doesn't make sense to me to bring a witness knowing that he won't finish his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It was only that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you substitute?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We cannot unfortunately because our witnesses are from the same area and it would be the same for all other witnesses that they would have to go back and to bring these witnesses is rather difficult. So the only possibility is if we finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Has 7.147 given evidence or is it this person that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it 7.147 that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No we are talking about witness 7.136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he's expected to last --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long in the witness box?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He is so-called background witness and Ms. Korner is calling him and so he expects to testify in chief for one day, and there will be some cross-examination, I am sure, that his testimony wouldn't finish in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you. I am not going to tell you what to do. It's not my decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's just information for that you if we decide not to call this witness, it would mean that we are not sitting on Friday, which I know Ms. Korner hates, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Even I hate it but I don't -- find me another solution. That's the problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this, Judge Janu -- I can understand that 7.144 may be required to be here at least two days or a day and a half in chief. Unfortunately, Mr. Ackerman is not here so we haven't got an idea of how long the cross would presumably last. What I can suggest before we jump to any conclusions or we take a decision is for your office to try -- or for you, Mr. Trbojevic, to contact Mr. Ackerman and see how long he expects his cross to last. Obviously if I were him I'm going to say it depends on what the witness will testify in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can communicate with him today and then let you know tomorrow. Mr. Ackerman will be here on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah but on Monday it will be too late because normally they will have brought the witness over the weekend. The way they do it, that's the way they do it. All right so we would appreciate if you could contact Mr. Ackerman at some point in time and we don't need to know. It's not that important for us to know exactly what the arrangements will be until we really come to that point, but the Prosecution would need to -- would need to know by tomorrow or by today evening today at the latest so that they can schedule his arrival or the postponement of his arrival. So I trust that there will be some contact made between you, Mr. Trbojevic, and Madam Richterova, and we will take it up from there. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it should be approached in two ways. First, how long it is expected to have this -- the cross-examination of this witness last, tentative guess, rough guess, and secondly also the other witness, because if the other witness is not expected to be here for more than one day, and Mr. Ackerman would think that he can cover the territory in his cross in the same day as the examination-in-chief, then perhaps we could think about it that way. Who will be conducting the in chief in the case of 7.136?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In both cases, it's Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask the Prosecution to tell us if the witness 7.136, who was scheduled for next Friday, does it mean that we are moving on to Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer this question. It means if we are calling the witness 7.136, that we will be dealing with this municipality but if we are not calling this witness on Friday, unfortunately we have to again reschedule the order of municipalities and it would be municipality of Donji Vakuf. We will let you know as soon as we decide about this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's fair enough. Another thing, Ms. Richterova -- Madam Richterova, you mentioned 7.6 as having already been granted protective measures. I am informed that he no longer insists on voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I forgot to mention it. He withdrew it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He is satisfied with facial distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's fair enough. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked about witness 7.136 because the Prosecution had announced that their next municipality would be Donji Vakuf rather than Prnjavor, and we have not been told anything about Prnjavor. We have not received a list of exhibits or other documents to be used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will be done -- it will be done. We can send it tomorrow by fax or by e-mail. It is ready and we only waited for this decision, which municipality will be called first, whether it is Prnjavor or Donji Vakuf. We apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. All right. Who do you want to start with? 7.95?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, we are starting with 7.95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go into closed session for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we remain in open session when he comes in?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It varies from courtroom to courtroom and I don't normally work in this courtroom so I don't know how it goes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Leave it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to speak the truth, and the whole truth. The text of the solemn declaration which is equivalent to an oath is contained in the piece of paper that the usher is going to show to you. Please read that aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be telling us the whole truth. Read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You may sit down. Let me explain to you very briefly what's going to happen. First of all, you have asked for and we have already agreed to grant you some protective measures. The first one is that you will not be referred to by your name and surname but by a nom de plume, a pseudonym that we have given you and you are going to be referred to as Witness BT50, BT50. You are a number for the purposes of this trial. Also, we have agreed to grant you facial distortion. In other words, no one will be able to see your face on any monitor or any TV outside this courtroom. Basically, if you are interested in seeing how this works and how you will appear to others, you just put your video mode -- your monitor on video mode and you will see what you look like. So that's by way of protective measures, and that's about it. Otherwise, the sitting, the session, will be in open and others will be able to follow the proceedings. Having said that, the only other two things remaining for me to explain is that you will first be asked a series of very short questions, if there are any, by Mr. Nicholls. That's in addition or by way of explanation of what you have already stated before in your statements to the Office of the Prosecutor. But the main feature of the day will be the questions that will be put to you on cross-examination by Mr. Trbojevic, who is the co-counsel defending Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. All right. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Nicholls, do you have any questions that you would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a few very quick ones, Your Honour, which deal with corrections or clarifications. First I would like to show the witness what's going to be Exhibit P1640 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir could you please read the name on that piece of paper quietly to yourself. Do not read it out loud and then confirm by saying yes or no whether that is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be Exhibit number P1640 and it is being tendered, received and will be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, please remember not to refer to your name. If you speak about any family members, you don't need to say their names either, because that might identify you. And I just want to put on the record and make clear you understand that you are testifying under the protections of image distortion and pseudonym and yesterday you told me that you did not require to have your voice distorted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'm going to ask you just a few questions about your statement which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on 12 December, 1998, just to make sure that everything is clear. You don't need to look at it right now but I'll refer to page numbers. On page 4, in paragraph 7, you referred to a person and it states Milan nickname Trnka. Could you tell me Milan nicknamed Trnka's last name, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Milan Balaban, also known as Trnka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So ever where in your statement where it may refer to either Milan Balaban or Trnka, that's the same person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On page 8, paragraph 3, of your statement, the name Radenko Balaban is written. Could you tell me if that's correct? Did you know a man named Radenko Balaban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you also refer in your statement to a man named Ranko Balaban, as the Josava SDS president. Is it correct that these are two different persons, two different individuals, with similar names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: No. They are brothers, two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. One brother is named Radenko, the other brother is named Ranko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was Radenko Balaban, if you know, a SDS member in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple more things I want to make clear. On page 4, paragraph 9, of your statement, it was stated that you saw a JNA facility whereas in fact, you heard about that JNA facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On page 5 n the last paragraph, you spoke about the expulsion or evacuation, the exodus from Suhaca as being on 25th of May, 1992, and I think you said yesterday you're not sure about that date; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Correct. If I may add, I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If you can tell us briefly, then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Since the 25th of May used to be the so-called -- the day of the youth in our country, we celebrated Tito's birthday one week prior to the 25th. So I think that that week was the 23rd of May -- that Sunday was 23rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The Sunday in which everybody left Suhaca you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, correct, when Suhaca was cleansed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: On page 5, paragraph 6, in your statement, it was stated that there was an agreement to allow the JNA or the military to search homes in Suhaca for weapons. Was there an agreement between the Muslims and the Serbs at that time to allow the searches of your homes -- of the homes in Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I'd like to say that there was no agreement. An order came to the effect that if we do not show up and hand in the weapons in the village of Maslovare, having left our houses unlocked, that the Suhaca would be shelled that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Finally, on the last paragraph of page 6, the statement describes a -- well, describes murders committed by Milan Balaban, nicknamed Trnka. It's not clear in the statement, I just want to make it clear for the Chamber, did you actually witness this murder, and if you did not witness it, why is it in your statement? How can you know that this is true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: We were amongst the last who were forced to go to the road in Blagaj. We were able to see the last lineup. I did not directly see the murder, but it happened a metre or two metres away from where I was. However, we were not allowed to look. A command was issued that whoever turned around would be killed, but I distinctly heard when Trnka took out these people, and I heard the shot. When we moved on I saw people lying on the ground. I hope this is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's clear. Those are the only clarifications I had, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Trbojevic? Now, sir, look at me, you are going to be asked questions by Mr. Trbojevic on cross-examination. You need to understand that Mr. Trbojevic is doing his duty here. He has a responsibility towards his client and that responsibility entails putting questions to you on cross-examination. And the consequence of all this is that you also have a responsibility towards your own conscience and towards justice and this Trial Chamber in that you must answer each and every question the same, in the truthful and clear manner in which you have answered or would have answered questions coming from the Prosecution. You have no right to distinguish between Defence and Prosecution as far as you are concerned. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'd like to try and clear certain issues stemming from your statement, the one that you gave on the 12th of December. You stated that you had not been active in politics, you had not belonged to any political organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: No. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement, in paragraphs 6 and 7, and on page 3, paragraphs 4 and 5, you enumerated all political officials, including the leaders, of the Suhaca chapter of SDA, also at the level of the municipality in Gornji Hozici, Donji Agici. How is it possible that you knew all these politicians so well, if you yourself were not politically active?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: You see, we live in small villages. It was a pre-war situation, and news travelled around very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were any jointly organised actions possible in those villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I'm not clear as to what you mean by "actions".

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring, for instance, to the meetings of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: There was no such a thing in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were any meetings organised at the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence had been withdrawn from the village of Donji Agici to Svodna before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The weapons were also withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes. As well as the equipment. There were no military formations whatsoever in our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: However, that was not the reason for people not to meet and plan what to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Well, people didn't meet at all. On the day when SDA representatives arrived, Mr. Resad and Mr. Dzafer and asked us to surrender all the weapons that we had, mostly hunting weapons, that's what happened. That was eventually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 8, you stated that a man by the name of Adem Barjaktarevic had fled to Croatia and had joined the BiH Army and fought as a member of the BH Army. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Fled is perhaps the wrong expression. His brother had a bus, he owned, privately owned a bus, and they were in transportation business. When the bridge in Bosanski Samac was destroyed, they could no longer come back because all roads were blocked and that he joined the BH army, this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is something that I heard only after I arrived in(Redacted)after the camp. And that he had also lost one leg in the battlefield. This is also what I heard in Germany. But I haven't seen him yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you wish to say that at the time in 1992, you were not aware of the fact that he had joined the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead now. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the last answer just to be careful, I'd like to redact the country mentioned, where the witness talked about going to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just to be on the safe side. I don't think it's that necessary but if you think it is necessary I will take your word. Please redact that. Go ahead. I'm sorry, to have had these interruptions. Mr. Trbojevic asked you the following question: Do you wish to say that at the time in 1992, you were not aware of the fact that he had joined the BH Army? The Bosnia-Herzegovina army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have not been possible for him to join the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information about the fact that some other people from your area intended to join the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: No. They could not have had such an intention. Our objective was to go on living peacefully with our neighbours. Nobody at the time was thinking about the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The fact remains, however, that a significant number of Bosanski Novi residents was in the area of Cazin in Buzinska Brigada for instance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Probably only after the cleansing and after the plight, but I don't know anyone who would have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 3 n the first paragraph, you make mention of Hamdija Huzejrovic, who is a Muslim, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that he was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any activities of his in terms of support to the SDS, that he would have provided?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I know only things that I heard from others and things that I saw while I was still in Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The same page, paragraph 3, you speak about the ethnic composition of the Bosanski Novi municipality. You say that 65 per cent of the population were Muslim, which, according to some information that we dispose of in this case, would not seem to reflect the reality. Are you sure about these particular data that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Believe me, this is something that I heard from others. As I said, I was not a member of any political organisation. I did not have any opportunity to have access to any documents or figures. So this is just information that at the time, after the elections, and just before the war, were discussed amongst the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In this part of your statement, it says that the SDA had won the election in Bosanski Novi, and that does not appear to be true either.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Again, this is what we were told, and in the Japra river valley, this was 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that a Serb was the President of the municipality after the elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: This is also what Sifet told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who the person was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did the name of the president of the municipality ever pop up in the negotiations that subsequently took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: There were no negotiations whatsoever. We were merely given orders through some kind of messengers, because those were some military men who made all kinds of requests when they came to our village. They wanted to see some Maljutkas, I don't know what kind of weapon that is. Which was then followed by disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Still on page 3 of your statement, you talk about the changes in personnel. You mention the commander of the police station, Huzejrovic, who was apparently dismissed. Can you be more precise in -- on this issue? Are we talking about the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You stated that these changes started in March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Huzejrovic was a police commander in Bosanski Novi -- actually, he was the commander of the police in Bosanski Novi and he was replaced, as was the case with others who were dismissed later on because they had not accepted uniforms bearing four Ss sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to separate these two issues. In March, 1991, at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the level of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, the coalition SDA, HDZ and SDS was fully operational, wasn't it? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That coalition was the one which put together the cabinet, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that coalition also provided the authorities in municipalities. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I wasn't into politics. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that on the basis of an interparty agreement, the personnel in all the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina were formed in this manner, would you agree with me or would you trust my words?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So that the reason for the dismissals in early 1991 had to be looked for in the results of the elections?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Object, Your Honour. I think he's answered this question, that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He wasn't into politics, he didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Whether you would trust my word that this is true, he doesn't know, I think he's answered the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, anyway, continue, Mr. Nicholls -- Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that in March, 1991, a number of executives were replaced, and he quotes the commander of the police station as an example. And I'm trying to remind him that that was the result of the interparty agreement, the coalition of the three ethnically based parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is only one more detail in that direction, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the spring of 1991, the minister of police, that is the Minister of the Interior, became Mr. Alija Delimustafic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is that it is the minister of police who appoints the commanders of police stations and chiefs of police in municipalities, and therefore, it was Alija Delimustafic who must have been the one who appointed the commander of the police station in Bosanski Novi in March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Sir, may I tell you -- may I say something to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be the first part of the changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the wake of the elections, in the Japra valley, there was no reserve police force because they had to turn in their weapons, and their gear, and the Japra valley and I had only the information that one could hear in the village, and when I tell you that an individual called Hamdija Krupic, who was with the police in Bosanski Novi, came in a -- came to Suhaca in a car, and said, "I'm getting away to the Sana. I've been fired," then you cannot expect from me to tell you something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to those uniforms with four Ss, as you said, I assume that, again, you do not have direct knowledge about that and that you merely said what you had heard from others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Not others, but those self-same policemen who had been -- who were fired because refused to wear uniforms with four Ss and it was common knowledge at the time, across the Bosanski Novi municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you ever see a police uniform with four Ss with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Do you mean at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: No, because they never came up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But could it be that you didn't see such uniform simply because such uniforms did not exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Well, I'll say something else to you. Whilst we still could go to the town, that is before the barricades, whilst the buses still ran, I had the opportunity to be in the town and see many things. How military forces crossed into Croatia, the whole town in camouflage uniforms, the withdrawal or the transit - I don't know really how to call it - of rocket launching systems towards Svodna, and I suppose everybody couldn't be but be quite clear about that. And besides, not only four Ss, but men dressed as Chetniks, with cockades -- and so on and so forth. And as they went to Croatia, the Serb people stood in a marketplace in Bosanski Novi, throwing cartons of cigarettes in their lorries, into their trucks and greeting them and I believe everybody saw that and I believe it stuck in everybody's memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that all that you tell us is true but a police uniform with four Ss, I put it to you that you could not see that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Sir, at that time, there were five or six different camouflage uniforms with all sorts of insignia, of all types.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he's answered the question already, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think so too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that you had been isolated and said that buses had stopped running, that you were not allowed to buy flour, sugar and other necessities, that you had to show your IDs if you wanted to go somewhere to do some shopping. This is on page 3, the one passage before last in B/C/S version. Could you please elaborate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, I could. Before -- well, I'll call them the Serb forces or our (Redacted) they felled the ash tree, the poplars, and they put them across the road to block the road. Trucks were being used and lorries, (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to redact the reference in that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obvious. Thank you, Mr. Nicholls, I was going to do that myself. But yes, please, we need to redact from, "I could buy it only because" right up to the very end. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic? Be careful not to say things in such a way that would expose your identity. Do you understand me? We are trying to protect you by hiding your name and hiding your face but you must be careful in what you say, that you don't use terms, names or references that could reveal your identity, such as you did just now, with your last question, by telling -- by mentioning who actually assisted you in procuring a sack of flour, all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is, but -- yeah, I'll do my best. But these are my emotions because such are the questions asked by the counsel. All I want is the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are only trying to help you in making the protective measures that we have granted you really effective. Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I asked for an explanation of this part of your statement, because as it is worded here, it seems to suggest that somebody might have prohibited from -- prohibited the sale of flour, sugar, et cetera, to members of the Muslim people. Were there any such prohibitions or is it a fact that there was a general shortage and therefore rationing had to be introduced? Perhaps that was the reason for the measures of control, because they were citizens from the territory of that municipality and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Nothing was being brought to the valley, and I was in specific situation, in a Serb locality, I was a witness to the fact that there, everything existed in sufficient supply, because goods were being brought by another itinerary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But isn't it a fact that the majority of privately owned shops were Muslim-owned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Every village had a shop which belonged to the agricultural cooperative in Donji Agici, and nothing was being delivered there either. And as for private shops --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, do you want to redact the sentence where the name of this village is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's all right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so too but I just asked you out of caution. All right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for private shops in the village, or villages, they simply couldn't get anything. They couldn't get any stocks. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did the gist of the question that is being put to you by Mr. Trbojevic basically would lead us to trying to find out from you whether the situation was the same or equally for the Muslims and other ethnicities. Was the situation the same for the Serbs, for example? Could they obtain flour and sugar and other necessities? Or was it a problem that was common to all the ethnicities in your area? This is the basically the question that Mr. Trbojevic has been putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs could have and did have everything, but we were cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also mentioned that there had been the Territorial Defence in the village of Donji Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And then that the weapons were pulled out as you told us today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And then you mentioned that a kind of a trade in weapons started, that is that the Serbs had tried to sell those weapons to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And for instance, the brothers Isakovic were selling weapons to Muslims presumably for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: That is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you thought that their liquidation next to the bridge perhaps had to do with the fact that they were taking part in this kind of trade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I do not know that. I don't know why they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You describe how you saw a helicopter land in the hamlet of Halilovici, and that some passenger cars approached it and reloaded weapons, you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Oh, that, yes, I saw the helicopter land, I saw those cars empty, going up there, and loaded returning. I did not see the weapons directly because the windows were covered with some sheets of paper or something, and I saw the helicopter fly off again. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason for the helicopter to land in Halilovici rather than some Serb village or hamlet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Sir, I said only what I saw, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: A while ago, you mentioned that there had been no negotiations about the turnover of weapons and that you were simply issued orders.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: That's right. A man came, and I believe he was Captain First Class, a man in his 50s, came and simply demanded that we do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 3, paragraph 4, B/C/S version, you say that two members of the SDA, Dzafer Kapetanovic and Resad Berberovic, met with the Serbs and that they said after that that you were to hand over your weapons. Could you tell us who is it that they met with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: I don't know. Those two gentlemen said that to us, that they had had a meeting of people in Suhaca and asked us to hand over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In fairness to the witness, I'd like to read the one sentence he makes in his statement about this because I think the way counsel phrased the question is not the same. We are talking about whether there were negotiations or whether this was an order to surrender weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's clear this up. Also, you need to be careful, Mr. Trbojevic, in the way you put words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could just read the sentence that the witness put in his statement, the witness states that the two representatives of "SDA members later came to the village to tell us that we had to surrender our weapons to the Serbs." That's the way it's phrased. I just want the witness to know what was in his statement, that it was not in his statement. It was implied that his statement said the words too -- in a much more equivocal language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish your question, Mr. Trbojevic, you've heard what Mr. Nicholls has said but perhaps we should let the witness have a copy of his own statement if he's going to be asked direct questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's right, I didn't request it yet because he's been doing very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we do it the proper way. We give him a copy of his statement and when you refer to what he stated in the statement, please refer to page and paragraph and line number, as you have been doing it so far, except for the last question. Yes. So now we are -- you are referring to the witness -- the witness to what page in the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5, passage 4, paragraph 4. That is what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You can find page numbers in the -- at the bottom, and we are talking about the paragraph which begins: "Our two members of the SDA Dzafer Kapetanovic and Resad Berberovic..." And you told us you didn't know who they were having a meeting with because that was what I wanted to ask you about. The next paragraph says two SDA members held meetings with Serbs at the municipal level in Bosanski Novi. "They mentioned no names but told us that they had talked with the military representative of the Serbs" have you found this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the -- that same meeting that was attended by Resad and Dzafer or is it a different meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: No. It was Dzafer and Resad who said that. When they came to our meeting and said that we had to hand over our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What is important for me is that a meeting was held with a military representative, as it says here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: That is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, it says, "Over the next few days, there were more rounds of negotiation. Sifet Barjaktarevic also took part in these negotiations. The outcome of these meetings was our surrender of the weapons. Those were hunting rifles, by and large. We went with those weapons to the village of Maslovare. It was agreed that the Serbs could search our houses looking for weapons, and if everything was all right, then we would be allowed to return." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there was a translation error. I do not know how is one to understand the word "negotiations" because they simply -- they would simply invite, summon Sifet to come, tell him what their request was, and he would convey it to the people in the village after his return. And as regards the word, "It was agreed that the Serbs could search our houses for weapons," I wish to amend this. We were ordered and told unless we all, down to the last one, came to Maslovare, and the tractor with all the weapons, with the tractor with all the weapons moving ahead of the column, and unless we left our houses opened and all our cupboards and wardrobes, unless we did that, (Redacted)would be shelled at 2.00. That was not an agreement. It was an order issued to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let us first clear this up. Was it recorded correctly here or was it misstated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there was a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But it's not one word which is wrong. There are two sentences here which mention negotiations and the thirds one speaks of an agreement or understanding.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Whatever -- whenever the agreements and understandings or negotiations are mentioned, that is wrong. Those were orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell us who uttered this order to bring a tractor with a -- carrying weapons and the threat that the village would be shelled at 2.00 and where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: (Redacted) there was no longer any passage. Husin Vranic had a shop there and he went with a convoy to try and purchase some flour. They took him back from Maslovare and said that if we do not show up, as I stated, with the weapons, all of 19 us, (Redacted)will be shelled. So it was this man who came on a truck to the village and he lives in sue ha Rijeka and told us that this is what they had told him. As to who directly told him this, I don't know. I don't know because in Maslovare armoured personnel carriers were left, were left behind, those who would later go to the village to do the search.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So that claim and that threat was conveyed to you by someone who had been stopped at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT50
utterances.text: Someone who was turned back, who was not allowed to continue to the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Stop one moment. Mr. Nicholls, in the last series of answers given by the witness, there is a reference to two villages. Does that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's right, Your Honour. I've been struggling with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Me too actually. It's quite undecided on whether to redact or not but if you prefer to play it safe, I think we ought to go for redaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think you're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in -- starting from page -- the beginning of page 55, Madam Registrar, right to where I put this interjection, please redact wherever there is a reference to the name of villages. There are two that I can recall. And I think both of them should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I don't know I think for this area of Mr. Trbojevic's cross-examination, maybe we should go briefly into private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would be easier for you, Mr. Trbojevic, too and easier for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, everybody can speak openly and I think we may be able --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a while but still what I indicated need to be redacted, Madam Registrar, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for having come over as I just stated on my own behalf and on behalf of the other two judges and on behalf of the Tribunal. You will now receive all the assistance you require to help you return to your country of residence. On our part we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break of 20 minutes. Is that okay with you, Mr. Trbojevic? And you, Mr. Nicholls and Madam Richterova? Do you think we will finish with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It depends on Mr. Trbojevic because I only have one question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour just before the witness leaves, I'd like to now tender the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tender the document, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: 1641, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's -- Mr. Brdjanin is here. Let's bring in the last witness for today. And it's pseudonym plus image distortion, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good. But we can remain in open session, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning -- good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start your testimony, may I ask you first to enter, make a solemn declaration, that is required by our rules, to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth? The text is contained in -- on a piece of paper that the usher is going to hand you now. Read that aloud and that will be your solemn declaration with us. It's equivalent to an oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Please sit down. I'll explain to you the procedure that we are going to follow today. It's a pretty simple one. We have your statement that you made to the Office of the Prosecutor and that will form the basis of your testimony. In fact, Madam Richterova for the Prosecution will only be asking you one question, because, as I explained to you, we have your statement already. But then you will be cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic who is the lawyer defending -- one of the lawyers defending Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin who is the accused in this case. Let's start with Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were granted protective measures of facial distortion and you will be referred to by pseudonym, by name -- by number. And now I would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like to show you a piece of paper on which your name is written. Read it for yourself and please just state yes or no, whether it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This would be Prosecution Exhibit under seal P1642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: As you heard, the judges know your statement, and I only want to ask you one thing, which is not clear from your statement, and it is when exactly you heard this announcement of -- to surrender your weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: It was the month of May, the exact date I'm not sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all that I wanted to clear up from his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Madam Richterova. Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you some questions seeking some explanation, if possible. You said that you worked in Dvor on the Una; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That was the Republic of Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And you were fired there because refused to join the army. That is what your statement says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please enunciate and wait for the counsel to finish his question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have the same problem again. Sir, look at me. You speak the same language as Mr. Trbojevic. And the consequence of that is that you are not even letting him finish his question. You're jumping with your answer straight away. But the thing is we don't understand your language. We have several persons behind the glass windows over there that are translating to us into English and into French. And they will have their task made much more difficult if you don't allow a short interval between question and answer. So please, I seek your cooperation, both of you, you and Mr. Trbojevic. Allow a short interval between question and answer. Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, the Prosecutor asked you about an invitation to surrender weapons. And you said that it was in May, 1992. Is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were Serbs also invited to hand over weapons that were not lawfully obtained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you say with certainty that neither over the radio, nor in the written press, were there any invitations to Serbs to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: How can you be so certain? Because we've had the opportunity here to see newspapers showing how at the joint meeting with Mr. Mehinovic and Mr. Dejanovic invited Serbs and Muslims to hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, can Mr. Trbojevic present evidence which he is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P -- Exhibit P1626?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the right-hand side towards the bottom of the page, there is a small article dated 8th of May. Can you see here the confirmation of what I said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, I see that but I think that such a confirmation is groundless. There was no such invitation to Serbs to hand down their weapons. I've never heard about it before. Not until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't need it any longer. In your statement, on page 4, paragraph 3, you speak about negotiations and your statement says, "Our representatives would go to Bosanski Novi, to agree about the manner in which the Muslims would leave the area. Two men represented us in these negotiations, Sifet Halilovic, president of the SDA from Suhaca, and Fikret Mehinovic, the SDA president from Hozici."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Maybe it would be easier for the witness if he has his statement so he can read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the first thing. Please hand the witness his statement. That's number 1. Secondly, do you want the -- this reference to the two persons and indication of where they came from to be redacted or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You have your statement, sir. Page 4, paragraph 3, I've just read to you the latter part of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Is that what this gentleman stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us additional explanation? What was the request of the Muslims to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: That was not a request made by Muslims. It was the request of the Crisis Staff in the municipality of Bosanski Novi that our representatives should report daily because we had to agree about the evacuation from the Japra valley, Blagaj and so on. That was the condition put to us by the Serb leadership in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What condition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: To leave the Japra valley, that is the expulsion of the Muslim population, of peasants, farmers, civilians, I don't know what to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean that one of those two Muslim representatives, after one of those meetings, notified the citizens that, as you put it, the Crisis Staff was requesting the Muslims to leave the Japra valley?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, that we had to leave it and the exodus lasted from May until July, until the Bosanski Novi municipality was finally evacuated, emptied, first with people going to Croatia and then to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've answered, you said that we would have to leave. I'm trying to get something more precise. I present to you the assumption, that the Muslims asked to leave and you said that no, you said that it was the condition. Now I'm asking you: Could you please clarify this? Was it the request of the Serb authorities or was it the conclusion reached by your representatives that no understanding could be reached and that you would eventually have to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: It was said that it had been agreed that we should leave because after all these meetings between the representatives in Bosanski Novi, Blagaj, Stari Agici, the Japra valley was shelled. Hozici and all the rest. There were searches, searches in Blagaj, Blagaj was evacuated as a village to the village of Maslovare, so that Japra and Blagaj could be searched, so that they could see -- as a matter of fact, they were mentioning some extremists who did not exist in the Japra valley and some weapons which we did not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Was your representative Sifet -- are you sure that his last name is Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I think it is, and that man was killed later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, on the same page, you describe how you personally saw how Sifet Halilovic was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I saw when a man took him towards the bridge and fired a round of -- and fired a round and the man fell and disappeared under the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And you do not know who was that individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, he was a military. I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, where were you watching it from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I watched it after I was put in a train car to go to Banja Luka, our final destination was the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about those stations later. But tell me now, how far was it between the railway car where you were and the place where Sifet and that soldier were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: It was about 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So you said this soldier let off a round of fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this soldier had an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: He had -- I guess an automatic rifle or some other automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Why do you say, "I guess"? Why do you say, "I suppose"? Presumably -- did you see the weapon that he fired from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I saw the weapon he fired from but I can't -- I can't really tell you which type of the automatic weapon it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't a light weapon, a small weapon, such as a pistol or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, you actually didn't see Sifet fall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because it was an embankment that was situated under the bridge, and it was from that embankment that he rolled down and fell under the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: So the soldier shot a burst of gunfire from an automatic weapon. How far was Sifet from him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Not very far, perhaps a metre or two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did he shoot him in the back, in the chest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I think he was shot from the back, in his legs. I think -- I'm almost sure that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And Sifet fell down the embankment and you could no longer see him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What happened when you joined the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: You mean when I got in the train truck?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: There was a huge number of people that crowded in. Names of individual people were called out and they were taken away. They did not get into the wagon. This roll call took place at the entrance, that is as we were getting in, getting on the train. Certain people were called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were the doors of the train shut at one point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Were they locked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I'm sure you know what a cattle wagon looks like. It is locked from the outside. You cannot open it from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: However, some of the cars were open?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: They were open while people were getting on. Once a train car was filled up, the doors would be shut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you trying to prove, Mr. Trbojevic? Because I'm getting curious now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, some witnesses testified that train cars were not locked, that they could open and shut the doors themselves. The train was not under any escort and it was possible to jump out whenever the train slowed down. They also testified that they got to Stanari but that some of them managed to leave the train before the soldiers arrived. So those who wished could disperse, and I think that these details are rather significant if we are discussing the issue of deportation. And whether it constituted a deportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You heard what Mr. Trbojevic has just explained. Were the trucks -- were the truck or the wagon in which you were, was it one of these type of trucks which you could open and close yourself at any time? Or was it the kind of cattle truck that you have just described that you can only open from outside? Forget about the possibility of other trucks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a kind of train whose cars could only be opened from the outside. That was the case of the one that I was in and the case of all other wagons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, where you eventually came to a halt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: In Stanari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: And who opened the doors of the train in Stanari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Serb soldiers, who had encircled the train, from a distance of about ten metres and it was the Serb soldiers who opened the doors of the train cars. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Then the separation of women and children from the men occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The men were returned to Novi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Not immediately. We were first detained in a room at the railway station where we waited for an excavator to dig out a hole because apparently we were going to be killed. It was only later that they loaded us on trucks. This lasted for quite a while, and all the while we were mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Who said that you were waiting for an excavator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: A soldier arrived and asked whether the hole had been dug out and this other soldier replied, "It will be soon."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the excavator digging the hole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: No, but one could hear the sound of the engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: However, this hole, if a hole was indeed being dug out, was never used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: No. We were loaded on to the trucks and 800 of us men were taken to Novi. The women had left for Croatia. For Otoka, I believe. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were 860 of us that were returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this is the exact figure but we were about 860. Those of us who were returned to the camp. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: How did you end up with this figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: The figure was mentioned during the roll call in the Mlakve camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Who guarded the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Serb soldiers. Under weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: How were you accommodated on the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: The accommodation was pretty bad. There was not enough space. We would sleep on the premises of the football club, in the offices, the changing rooms, on the stairways and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that there was a -- not enough space. However, a football stadium should have sufficient space, a sufficient number of rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes, but we were not allowed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: There were changing rooms, right? Did you use them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Two rooms were used, and you know what a changing room looks like for football players to change and shower. There was a toilet for all of us but the rooms itself -- the rooms themselves were not very large and the floor was made of concrete. They still exist. We did not use all of the premises. We were only allowed to use some of them. And that space was not very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were allowed to use only one toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: There was only one toilet in that part of the stadium where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: A football stadium is supposed to have toilets for visitors as well as toilets for players.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: I'm telling you that there was only one toilet that we were allowed to use, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was no water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have any water before we were registered. Taps would be shut from time to time. There was no water for us to wash or to bathe. We all had lice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Surely a football stadium must have all the necessary facilities for washing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: It does, sir. However, the water that we had was brought to the stadium in tanks and it was an ice-cold water that we had to shower with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned as a form of mistreatment at the stadium that they made you eat grass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it really grazing or was it that you had to pluck weed and work on that green area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT87
utterances.text: No. One of the soldiers who had a gun in his hand forced us to do it, and that is how we interpreted what he told us, and most of us obeyed. We didn't have anything to eat, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness, very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Trbojevic, for your cooperation. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is no re-examination. I only want to tender the statement of this witness as Prosecution Exhibit P1643.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is so being admitted. So that brings us to the end of your testimony, sir, for which I thank you, both on my own behalf and on behalf of the two judges that sit together with me, Judge Janu from the Czech Republic and Judge Taya from Japan. We also thank you for having accepted to come over to the Hague to this Tribunal to give evidence. You are free to return back to your country of residence and you will receive all the assistance you require from the officers of this Tribunal. On our part, the only thing left for us to say is that we wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, usher, you can accompany the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The very last thing I only want to confirm we are not hearing this witness 7.263 because she declined to testify and so we do not have any witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And Monday, we are starting with 7.144, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Exactly, 7.144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it it's no longer going to be in closed session although we had already granted closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We just received confirmation that it can be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please inform Mr. Ackerman about that, all right? And if you can get some kind of feedback from Mr. Ackerman about the points raised by me earlier on, pass them on to the Prosecution straight away, all right? Thank you. So have a nice weekend and we will all meet on Monday, I think in Courtroom III, if I remember well. It's a whole week in the morning. We will not be sitting on Tuesday. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
